items.text: The frame: "Our ageing population is a bigger threat than climate change", because of the cost of living, pressure on health services and societal tensions (slide 2).

Ageing is malleable: in England (ONS, 2018 to 2020, in the Chief Medical Officer's Annual Report 2023), the least deprived 10% of small areas live 70.7 years in good health and 15.6 in poorer health; the most deprived 51.9 and 26.4 (slide 5).
Three fundamentals of ageing: the rate of ageing accelerates with time, variation between individuals increases, and homeostasis declines (slide 6).
Trials to slow ageing need large numbers and several years, ideally in people who are healthy but ageing, and funding and approval are challenging (slide 7).
The call to action: make the case for healthy longevity, make trials long enough to measure ageing, and have industry, charities, government and universities work together (slide 9).
Milestone: "the first year in which we have spent more physically on prevention than we have on treatment", and the gap between supplements and OTC will widen [00:20] (photo 2).

Money is moving to premium dietary supplements, through line extensions, brand actions and M&A; he sees "about eight to $9 billion in motion", some from venture capital and private equity outside health [00:20].

Healthspan as a funnel: the edge (SKU names directly on age and life stage, including mitochondrial) is niche, growing and earns a premium; broader healthspan wording appears on cheap and expensive products alike; protection messages (immune, antioxidant) cover about half the shelf [00:20].

Ingredient life cycle: proof of benefit, then premium, then popularity, then price war. Magnesium forms "turned into footballs" on price, while L-threonate, the cognitive form, still holds a premium; "popularity is the death knell on premium" [00:20] (photo 3).

NAD+ is losing its premium as it goes mainstream (US price index 1.84 in 2024, 1.43 in 2026 to date); postbiotics lead what queues behind it, with share up 48% and a price index of 2.83 [00:20] (photo 4).
IM8 is the fastest year-one growth he has seen: one product of 90 ingredients positioned to replace 16 supplements, with year-two revenue guidance of USD 220 to 230 million [00:20] (photo 7).

Concern about ageing starts younger: retired respondents mostly began thinking seriously about it in their 60s (36%); in the deck's version of the chart, people working full-time mostly began in their 30s (about 30%, read from the chart). She called it "a generational shift" [00:04] (photo 1) (slide 4).

The younger the respondent, the less they credit genetics and the more they credit supplements: genetics from 39% at 65 plus down to 21% at 18 to 24; supplements from 20% at 25 to 34 down to 12% at 65 plus [00:04] (slide 2) (slide 3).
One in four is actively pursuing anti-ageing: 16% want to prevent premature ageing and 11% to reverse it, beside 52% who want to age slowly and healthily [00:04] (photo 2) (slide 5).

Energy, stamina and strength is in the top three concerns of every age band, for men and women; mobility, joint and bone health is in the top three of every band from 35 to 44 up for both, and from 25 to 34 for women (photo 3) (slide 8).

Trust is the gap. Biggest hesitation about longevity supplements in the UK: not enough proof 22%, cost 21%, don't believe claims 20%, safety concerns 20%. Across the survey, 36% already take supplements to counteract natural ageing [00:04] (slide 17) (slide 18).

Brands are moving from product to platform: Niagen added telehealth, IV and injections, skincare and a drug pipeline; Life Extension sells ageing blood tests to take before and after supplements; Novos sells an at-home biological-age kit [00:04] (photo 4) (slide 9) (slide 19).

Holland & Barrett created a longevity category in store over the last six months; it is "still quite small" but has seen "really significant growth", driven primarily by NAD, with spermidine less popular [02:58] [03:47].

items.text: In animal studies, rodents without a microbiome live longer. He said normal mice live about 25 months and germ-free mice almost ten months longer [00:24]. In the 1991 study on his slide, mean lifespan was 88.9 weeks germ-free against 75.9 weeks conventional on a full diet, and 117.5 weeks, the longest, for conventional mice on a restricted diet (slide 6) (slide 7).

Observational studies link healthy dietary patterns to healthy ageing, with the Alternative Healthy Eating Index performing "consistently best" (slide 8). A UK study is titled "Life expectancy can increase by up to 10 years following sustained shifts towards healthier diets" (slide 9); he described it as ten years of healthier lifespan, and "probably" five to six years if the shift comes in the 70s [00:24].

His Cell trial of the non-industrialised "Restore" (NiMe) diet, 45 g of fibre a day, against participants' usual diet: LDL cholesterol down 16.8% (he said 17%), glucose down 6.3%, CRP down 14.0%, BMI down 1.4%; faecal pH and the ratio of branched-chain to short-chain fatty acids also fell [00:24] (slide 14) (slide 15).

Bifidobacterium adolescentis falls with age and is linked with healthy ageing: it peaks at about 4.8% of the gut microbiome around age 40 in healthy people (read from the chart, Synbiotic Health's data on 8,942 people), it was the strongest predictor of slower epigenetic ageing in 123 adults, and in animal studies it improved healthspan and lifespan. Synbiotic Health's human trials in older people are ongoing, with no data yet [00:24] (slide 17) (slide 20) (slide 21).

His take-home: the gut microbiome is a plausible contributor to healthy ageing, "but human causality remains incompletely established"; complementary microbiome-targeted interventions are promising, but clinical trials are needed [00:24] (slide 22).

He is doubtful that a postbiotic can change gut ecology or raise short-chain fatty acids, prefers probiotic bifidobacteria with fibre, and sees a possible role for postbiotics in a direct immune effect [22:01] [22:52].

Naturalness opens the conversation: Robert listens more the more natural the product and shuts off at pills [23:46], Matt and Mike said much the same [24:01] [24:34], and Robert named naturalness as the main thing to build into a new product [45:44]. Rahav was the exception: she does not mind non-natural products if she is told how they help her [47:02].

Proof decides: Michelle wants the science and a dose high enough to be effective [25:28] [25:59], Nadine wants to know whether the research was independent or paid for by a company with a vested interest [31:00], Mike wants clinical trials on the brand's site [42:40], and Rahav wants trials to say honestly whom they were not tested on [43:43].

Trust comes from time and brand: Mike and Kane trust Holland & Barrett because it has been around a long time [24:34] [31:45]; a new brand, Mike said, needs a mix of advertising, proof on its site and a brand story, and cannot be built overnight [42:40] [47:44].

Influencers are distrusted: Matt avoids health advice from social media [18:23], Mike asks "what's in it for them" [42:40], and Kane said what works for an influencer may not work for him [31:45]. Their sources are friends, Ayurvedic doctors, an Instagram feed and a Netflix documentary on Blue Zones [10:12] [17:45] [16:37] [20:32].

AI is used with checks: Mike asks ChatGPT and Claude for evidence and checks it on Google [36:58], Rahav uses AI for low-stakes questions only [38:15], Nadine said AI has to be verified [38:53], and Matt ignores AI on health [37:33].

Collagen needs a reason today: Rahav wants a collagen pitch to explain why she needs it when her great-grandmother did not [26:18], and Donella wants to know what to take with collagen and where it comes from [28:18].

Calorie restriction: in a 14-year lifetime study in dogs, 25% calorie restriction against pair-fed controls gave a median life span of 13 years against 11.2, "+ 15% longer life", with better insulin sensitivity and immune function and later disease onset (Lawler et al., 2008) (slide 4).

Weight and biological age, unpublished: biological age (PhenoAge) rises with BMI, weight loss in people with obesity lowers it, and meal-replacement regimens lowered it with weight loss, against baseline at weeks 26 and 52 (read from the chart) (slide 5).

Creatine is the first of four "Examples of supplements to improve mitochondrial functions", with nicotinamide riboside, urolithin A, and N-acetylcysteine and glycine, each shown beside a Solgar or Pure Encapsulations pack (slide 7).

Muscle: nicotinamide and vitamin B6 activated muscle stem cells and enhanced regeneration in a human RCT, with 29% more activated Pax7+ cells and 37% more regenerating myofibres against placebo; the deck says there is no direct mitochondrial mechanism (slide 8) (slide 9).

NAD+: two weeks of daily nicotinamide riboside (1 g) or NMN (1 g) raised blood NAD+ against placebo; nicotinamide (0.5 g) did not. The route runs through low absorption and conversion by gut microbes (Christen et al., Nature Metabolism 2026) (slide 10).

Thymol (20 mg/kg a day) lowered biological age, improved running distance, preserved grip force and raised the mitophagy protein Pink1 in fast-ageing SAMP8 mice; his translational verdict is that more evidence in humans is needed (slide 13) (slide 15).

Selman's case, all from worms and mice: mitochondrial function falls with age, and reduced nutrient sensing, a 30% calorie cut and NMN each preserved it in mice; NMN made mitochondria more efficient without adding more of them (slide 5) (slide 7) (slide 8) (slide 9).

Long-term NMN (about 550 mg/kg a day in drinking water from 13 months of age) is shown reducing frailty in both sexes and extending female lifespan in mice; the source is a 2024 bioRxiv preprint, and the frailty chart is labelled schematic, its values illustrative (slide 10).

UTHEVER's published trial (Frontiers in Aging, 2022): 66 adults aged 40 to 65 randomised, 62 analysed, 300 mg a day for 60 days; the slide reports a 38% increment in NAD+ levels and 6.5% gains in walking endurance and quality of life, read from the slide image, without saying whether against placebo (slide 13).

The sleep trial (EffePharm data on file): 34 adults aged 30 to 60, 600 mg a day or placebo for eight weeks. At day 56 the NMN group scored lower than placebo on sleep quality (PSQI, p<0.05), insomnia severity (ISI, p<0.01) and fatigue (FS-14, p<0.05); within the group the scores fell 36.61%, 48.43% and 48.15% from baseline (slide 14) (slide 15) (slide 16) (slide 17).
Deep sleep rose 27.65 minutes (38.88%) against the NMN group's own baseline (p<0.05); no placebo comparison is shown (slide 18).

EU novel food: filed August 2023, public consultation completed February 2025, positive EFSA safety assessment published May 2026, approval "expected" in November 2026; the US FDA sent an NDI no-objection letter in November 2025, and the UK application is in progress (slide 20) (slide 21).
In the studies she cited, people on GLP-1 medicines absorbed paracetamol 15 to 50 percent less; absorption studies that leave them out are "not you know, collecting the right data" [00:00].

Study populations do not match buyers: a typical pharmacokinetic study is on a 25-year-old, while longevity products are typically sold to 65-year-old women on three medications, with low oestrogen and a history of antibiotics [00:00].
Look at responders and at high and low absorbers, not only at a rise in the blood: "did 90% of people get that?" [00:00].
Test products as they are taken: most pharmacokinetic studies are fasted and single-dose, while real users eat, drink coffee, miss doses and stack medications [00:00].
Long-term trials should measure blood levels as well as outcomes, now that home tests are easy; some nutrients, such as iron and vitamin D, need longer studies [00:00].
On dose, a five-dose pharmacokinetic study early is "easier and honestly cheaper" than five doses in a long-term study; she suggested lower doses for longer [05:14].
Thorne's own survey, as Manor gave it: roughly 40% of consumers use AI for health questions, and two out of three would use an AI tool they trusted to make decisions [00:23].

items.text: Chen said Radicle Science has put about 100,000 people through double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trials in about six years, and is running a US-government-funded mental health trial of 6,000 people with one shared placebo and 19 treatment arms [34:11].

Guardrails against hallucination: ALT keeps AMBROSIA from going outside the literature [36:40]; Thorne monitors and scores every Taya message and sends flagged ones to regulatory and medical [37:43]; Chen said narrow knowledge bases and checking agents cut the risk [39:03].

Chen: home kits, wearables and phones let decentralised trials collect data sites cannot; agents can automate the "multi-100-step process" of a trial, and machine learning is needed to read the data [39:58]. Biomarkers, wearables and surveys each show one part, so he wants them combined [43:09].

Small studies: an audience member said many industry studies are pilots of 45-50 or 100 people [58:46]; Spagnuolo said nutraceutical trials run to tens or hundreds, against tens of thousands in pharma [59:13]; Chen said the FDA and NIH are shifting funding toward decentralised approaches [59:31].
Spagnuolo called for publishing what did not work, since "There's no journal of unpublishable results" [53:38].
Chen sees a new chance for brands to show consumers, with their own data, that a product delivers its promise [1:02:46].

Longer lives, not healthier ones: the gap between lifespan and healthy years is 2.4 years wider for women than for men across 183 countries, and women spend 25% more of their lives in poor health (slide 5).

items.text: Starbucks' 15 g protein cold foam is his example of the bigger market: Starbucks say one in seven coffees now provides 15 g of protein. A bigger market is not more of the same market [00:00].

Brands are not just mitigating whey prices but going through a "structural reset". New products that cut whey reliance and a shift into creatine, energy and fibre are the "top priority for brands" [00:00] (photo 6).

More "whey hybrids" (sold as whey, blended with milk, soy or yeast to cut cost) launched in the last 12 months than ever; whey milkshakes and whey plus collagen are the next pillars [00:00] (photo 9).
Plant protein still underdelivers on taste. It should sell itself as a very good protein, not as plant [00:00] (photo 10).
Gummies are the fastest-growing creatine format by new launches: 8.0% of creatine products, 36.2% of them added in the last six months, with "lots of conjecture about stability" [00:00] (photo 14).
A quarter of creatine products use a branded ingredient, most of it from one supplier, and he said there is a race to follow; pre-workout is highest at 53% [18:50] (photo 27).
The core constraint: cheese production grows about 1.5% a year, while whey protein demand grows over 10%. He called it the most important conclusion of the talk [00:16] (photo 7) (slide 5).
Producers chose isolate. Over five years WPI grew 15.0% a year and WPC80 1.5%; clear WPI is now about a quarter of all isolate (photo 9) (slide 8).
Between 25 August and 4 November 2026, WPC80 fell 40.7% to €16.00/kg and WPI 20.3% to €25.50/kg, while MPC85 rose 13.5% to €15.80/kg (photo 18) (slide 12).
New capacity will not close the gap: he forecast WPI at 7 to 11% a year and WPC80 at 4 to 7% to 2030, and both cannot reach the top of their range [00:16] (photo 11) (slide 9).
Mainstream buyers choose on taste and texture, not protein source, and whey is the easiest protein to make taste good [00:16].
For buyers: "Don't try to time the market. Keep inventory steady. Whey will be expensive." (photo 20) (slide 13)
More than 1,000 misleading food posts by influencers were counted in a recent report, with supplements the most frequent subject [00:01].

Tonic runs itself as "a media business that happens to sell vitamins": 99% of its content is not about its products, and it has 1.9 million followers and about 70 million views a month [01:00], [03:24].
AG1 found that talking about trials and third-party testing did not land: "people didn't care". Too much evidence fails at the top of the funnel; the science sits mid-funnel [04:17], [18:30].

Clearcast rejected "the best version of you", "a better version of you" and "a slightly better version of you" before approving "Ever wondered what life would be like with a little extra help?" Julian's lesson: "creative constraint is a very powerful way to deliver better communication" [18:30].
Brands bear most responsibility for their influencers' health claims in most jurisdictions; the answer is training, contracts and briefing [28:27].
Athletes are "probably the most impressionable group": they believe a claim of "up to 10% better performance" applies to them personally [32:33].
The evidence gap: of 5,261 publications with 12,511,386 participants, 63% studied males and females, 31% males only and 6% females only (Cowley et al., 2021) (slide 4).

Even when women are included, 14% of performance supplement studies defined menstrual status and about 0.5% verified it with best-practice methods; female participation rose from about 39% (2011-13) to about 44% (2021-23) (Smith et al., 2022; Ose et al., 2025) (slide 6).

The cycle and performance: 13 of 16 studies found no effect on anaerobic performance and 14 of 22 none on aerobic performance; no influence of phase on strength or training adaptations, "BUT motivation could be impactful" (Carmichael et al., 2021; Colenso-Semple et al., 2023). A review found the evidence does not warrant general guidance on changing exercise across the cycle (McNulty et al., 2020) (slide 15) (slide 16).

Nutrition: carbohydrate targets are per kg of body mass and apply to both sexes, with no evidence for phase-specific targets; energy intake tends to rise about 170 kcal a day in the luteal phase. The primary focus is adequate energy intake and optimal energy availability (ISSN position stand, Sims et al., 2023) (slide 18) (slide 19).

Protein: high-quality protein as close to the start and/or end of exercise as possible at 0.3-0.4 g/kg body weight, aiming for the upper end in the luteal phase "due to the catabolic actions of progesterone" (Sims et al., 2023) (slide 20).

Building better products: include only ingredients with evidence for the outcome claimed, "e.g. creatine 3–5 g/day alongside strength training for midlife muscle and strength"; use trial doses, list every dose, batch-test for athletes (e.g. Informed Sport); use authorised claims; co-design with women and fund female-specific studies (slide 23).

Women started with less muscle glycogen than men but finished similarly depleted. The gap was under 5 g in the gastrocnemius, comes from dosing per kilogram, and has no practical bearing on guidelines [00:00].
At 120 g of carbohydrate an hour, the crossover from carbohydrate to fat was completely prevented over two hours, in both sexes; at 60 g it came after about an hour [00:00] (photo 4) (photo 6).

Men and women oxidise carbohydrate taken during exercise at comparable rates, rising with dose (120 > 90 > 60 g); at 120 g some individuals oxidised 80 to 100 percent of what they took [00:00] (photo 7).
Running economy improved by two to 3% at 120 g an hour, against the 4% Nike claimed for the Vaporfly; he is "pretty sure" this is part of why running records are falling [00:00] (photo 9).
Women reported more gastrointestinal symptoms, "which may be due to anatomical differences in colon length"; individual variation warrants personalised fuelling [00:00] (photo 9).
The biggest barrier is educational, in a world where under-fuelling has been prevalent; he does not believe in fuelling to the menstrual cycle [00:00] (photo 20).

Brands have three responses to whey costs: raise the price, shrinkflation, or smarter formulation with protein blends, which she called the most elegant and a way to stand out on shelf [00:10] (slide 5).

Launches combining whey and collagen grew at 17.44% a year from 2023 to 2026 to date, led by snacks, cereals and energy bars (39.7%) and nutritional and meal replacement drinks (36.4%); her example, Optimum Nutrition's clear whey isolate with collagen, has 10 g of each [00:10] (slide 6).
Collagen supply is spread across bovine, porcine, chicken and fish, and its historical prices fluctuate far less than whey's [00:10].
Whey and collagen are "no competitors": whey for muscle, Peptan (rich in hydroxyproline, glycine and proline) for ligaments, tendons, joints and bone [00:10] (slide 8).

In 22 men over three weeks of training, 25 g whey plus 20 g Peptan a day gave the same recovery and performance as 45 g whey; the slide says such blends "may provide broader support across the musculoskeletal system" [00:10] (slide 9).

2 × 10 g Peptan a day with vitamin C, for a week before 150 drop jumps and two days after, gave 28% less muscle soreness and 13% faster muscle recovery than placebo; the slide marks the soreness result as a likely benefit and the recovery result as significant [00:10] (slide 10).

Three segments of everyday athlete: "inspired by" (habits, feeling better, food first), "driven by" (measured progress, nutrient timing around training) and "live by" (optimisers who plan the whole 24 hours around training) [00:54].
Most of their 8,000 daily training-app users train at 6:00 in the morning, so Marchon put carbohydrate into a pre-workout for people who will not eat toast or porridge first [00:54], [04:00].
Awareness is high but understanding lags: gym-goers talk confidently about products they saw in an ad without knowing why, so "education is really critical at this stage" [05:29].
Liam: creatine is "here to stay" and the research is moving into cognition; for ingredient suppliers the challenge is format, meaning stability in water, gummies and other formats [08:24].
When Marchon surveyed its gym members, the number one struggle was still hitting their daily protein requirement [16:50].
Five years out, Liam's bet is "formats that improve compliance": gummies, jellies, powders, RTDs, and convenience [22:11].

The dose problem: guidance from fruit-polyphenol studies is about 300 mg 1 to 2 hours before exercise for performance and over 1,000 mg a day for at least 3 days around hard exercise for recovery, but the slide asks "mg of what?" (slide 3). A label figure can mean total polyphenols, a subclass or one compound; his three questions for any ingredient are which compound, how much and measured how (slide 5).

Mechanism: blood levels are too low for polyphenols to act as direct antioxidants; they act as signals. Of five mechanisms, only increased blood flow (nitric oxide) is rated "consistent" in humans; the others are rated limited, mostly animal, inconsistent or mostly lab (slide 6).

The big four: blackcurrant has the strongest evidence for performance and cherry for recovery; pomegranate (performance) and turmeric (recovery) are equivocal; 3 of the 4 share anthocyanins as a main polyphenol (slide 7).

The lesson from nitrate and Nomio: make the dose and timing the message, and let credible users do the teaching. Beetroot nitrate became "one shot, 2–3 hours before and/or for 1 week prior to competition" (slide 11).
A layered label: "Rich in polyphenols" on the front for awareness, "X mg anthocyanins per serving, standardised and batch tested" on the back for credibility (slide 12).
His three asks of the industry: standardise and declare, fund the right trials (trained athletes, women, blood levels, real outcomes) and communicate dose and timing (slide 13).

Carbohydrate is "a Signal, Not Just a Substrate": its availability is "an electrical green light" telling the body it is metabolically safe to invest in bone remodelling, iron handling and endocrine function (slide 3) (slide 4).

Quick against quiet costs: a glycogen deficit shows as a flat session and heavy legs, usually fixed within a day of good fuelling; bone, iron and hormones give no immediate signal, and by the time a bone stress injury, low ferritin or menstrual dysfunction appears the debt has been building for weeks (slide 5).

Bone markers: carbohydrate during running significantly reduces the acute rise in the resorption marker CTX, and carbohydrate with protein after exercise alters bone turnover markers favourably; about 3.5 weeks of a ketogenic diet in race walkers raised resorption and suppressed formation, with incomplete recovery once carbohydrate was restored. The slide notes these are acute responses over hours, mostly in men (Sale et al., 2015) (slide 8).

The hidden risk zone: short-term carbohydrate restriction suppresses bone formation more than low energy availability does, so energy intake alone will not flag bone risk and practitioners must screen for carbohydrate availability (Heikura et al., 2020; Fensham et al., 2022) (slide 10).

Timing: even with an identical daily total, within-day energy deficiency is linked to unfavourable hormonal profiles in female and male athletes (Fahrenholtz et al., 2018); "Daily totals cannot save a back-loaded schedule" (slide 12) (slide 20).

Iron: a hard endurance session triggers an IL-6 spike and hepcidin rises over 3-6 hours; low carbohydrate availability amplifies this, "functionally blocking iron absorption", so iron-rich meals and supplements should be timed around carbohydrate-restored windows (slide 13).
In the UK, 6.1% currently use GLP-1s, 5.7% have used them and 15.1% are considering them: almost 27% of the population, c.18.4 million people (slide 8) [00:08].

Current UK users are not the obesity population the drugs were designed for: 56% female, 63% Gen X or Millennial, 63% ABC1 (slide 10), and 74% happy to pay more for quality against a 70% average (slide 11).

Among European current users (n=352), 57% increased their supplement use, 88% including no change. Proteins lead at 51%; creatine is at 27%, above HMB at 15% (slide 13). He had said "near 60%" and "near 90%", and creatine was "maybe slightly higher" than expected [00:08].

The most common challenges on the drugs: fear of weight regain 30%, side effects 29%, cost 29%, reduced food enjoyment 27%, maintaining nutrition 22%, muscle loss concerns 22% and difficulty consuming enough protein 19% (slide 14).

78% of users are confident of keeping the weight off (94% including neutral), yet the BMJ study on his slide found regain almost four times faster after stopping the drugs than after diet and physical activity changes (slide 15, read from the slide image).
Putting GLP-1 on pack is "a kind of a health claim", so retailer support such as Boots' GLP-1 bays matters [00:08] (slide 17).
GLP-1 drugs give weight loss of "between five to 15%" [00:15]; his table gives 3.6% for liraglutide, 11.4% for semaglutide and 15.0% for tirzepatide (slide 17).

Up to 50% of users have GI symptoms and about 40% of the weight reduction comes from lean body mass (slide 20). He said muscle loss "can lead to sarcopenia" [00:15]; his slide lists sarcopenia with "insufficient evidence" (slide 20, read from the slide image).
Proteins have an "undisputed effect" on GLP-1 secretion; high-protein meals trigger GLP-1 and PYY, and the effect depends on the amino acid profile, such as leucine [00:15] (slide 23).

Berberine, cinnamon and bitter compounds have mechanisms but "mild to modest" effects and few human studies; berberine "does not directly bind to or activate GLP-1 receptors" [00:15] (slide 25) (slide 26).

In his centre's APPETITE trial (12 participants; porridge alone, with potato protein or with whey protein), both proteins gave a comparable, significant increase in GLP-1 secretion (slide 28) (slide 30).

In the SATISPHY trial of Reducose (40 participants), post-meal GLP-1 rose 140% and appetite fell 23% against placebo, with "a marked reduction in appetite as well as food noise"; both trials are unpublished, manuscripts in progress (slide 31) (slide 33).
Brett: GLP-1 trends are "accelerations of existing macro trends", and retailers now want sports nutrition across the supermarket, not only on the health fixture [28:46].

Few products put GLP-1 overtly on pack: Myprotein builds need-state bundles rather than a labelled GLP-1 range, and Boots' "GLP-1 friendly" bays let it be present without the wording [29:57], [30:32], [51:57].
Brett: clear protein is "performing extremely well" in retail, and clear protein plus collagen is "just a sweet spot for this this consumer", with retail launches coming [35:09], [43:51].
Nick: plant protein's barrier is taste; it has got better but is "never quite as good as we truly expect for the majority of people" [37:08].
Nick: creatine has become "almost like a tier one ingredient", adopted by women, ageing consumers and weight-management users [38:42].
Ed: people who simply eat less risk missing key nutrients, with a risk of RED-S and deficiencies; for low appetite he puts protein first, then carbohydrate, then micronutrients [32:49], [34:13].

The frame: lifespan is how long we live, healthspan how long we avoid disease, "Peakspan" how long we stay close to our personal best; consumers rank mobility, staying active and an active mind as the top three aspects of healthy ageing (Innova survey, 11 countries) (slide 4).

items.text: The test: of two real enquiries a year apart, the human one spots that zinc and iron cannot be combined, admits the gap and asks for a meeting; the AI-written one asks for everything at once. Her verdict: "Perfect form ≠ understanding." (slide 2) (slide 14) (slide 15)
Expertise is understanding, not the amount of information held; it lives where people and processes inside a company meet customers, change and credible sources outside it (slide 12) (slide 13).

Information floods in from seminars, conferences and AI; critical thinking (verifying sources and context) filters it to the essence, and without the filter speed rises and understanding falls (slide 17).

The way out: understand, "feel it = want it", question the assumption, adapt. Inertia, "repeating what I already know", is the enemy; pause before the next course or tool and ask what you need (slide 19).
What Favea does about it: validation of enquiries (a revised internal process), verification of sources, and quality by expertise (slide 20).
One tip for Monday: when a perfect email arrives, pick up the phone (slide 22).

Creatine launches rose 61.9% in January to August 2026 against January to August 2025; over 2022 to 2025 they grew +35.6% against +11.1% for the average ingredient (Innova Market Insights; Vita Actives analysis) (slide 2).
Retail price per kg of creatine, medians: €73 plain unflavoured powder, €87 flavoured powder (1.19×), €222 combination powder (3.03×), €275 formats such as gummies (3.76×) (slide 2).

Beyond performance: pack claims on creatine launches, 2025 to 2026, hydration +107.1%, health and wellness +78.2%, brain and mood +61.5%, energy and stamina +60.0%, women-specific +400.0% (base below 10); creatine launches in the supplements aisle outside sports nutrition +194.7%; the EU-authorised claim for strength with training in adults over 55 is rarely used on pack (slide 3).

Combinations grew 134.0% in 2026 against 52.7% for creatine on its own; the fastest partners are electrolytes +101.2% (hydration), magnesium +138.9% (sleep and overnight recovery), collagen +80.0% (recovery, skin and joints), and HMB and citicoline from a base below 10 (slide 4).

Flavoured launches rose from 38.4% to 66.6% of creatine launches from 2022 to 2025, yet 82% of products on the shelf are still a single unflavoured SKU; in 2026 bars grew +260.0%, chewables +250.0%, powder +62.4% and gummies +29.5% (slide 5).

Quality: 18 of 88 creatine gummies failed their label claim in independent testing and 10 contained no creatine (ABENUTRI 2024); in the only published market survey, half of commercial creatine failed at least one EFSA limit (Moret et al., 2011) (slide 6) (slide 7).

On 265 product pages assessed, energy and vitality is the most common message (83.8%), while the hallmarks of ageing are named on 9.1% and placed in lead copy on 4.2% (slide 5); spoken as about 300 products, 9% and 4% [00:00].

Price: median price per serving in capsules and tablets is €0.47 for creatine (518 products) against €1.35 for longevity (194) and €1.36 for NAD (28), read from the chart (slide 7); spoken as "around about 50 cents" for creatine [00:00].
MitoQ Longevity Creatine Complex, 5 g creatine with citicoline, sells at €1.60 a serving, 3.41 times the creatine median, positioned for "muscle, mind and cellular energy" (slide 7).
"You don't sell one product in 2026": Cellaro Core is three products, one system (morning, evening, a monthly two-day reset) (slide 6) [00:00].

Longevity 2.0: precision and convenient formats (a spermidine pen, an NAD+ liquid, longevity chocolate), hydration with a cellular-health story (DryWater), and longevity as a performance story (Centenarian Road) (slide 8) [00:00].

PeptiStrong is a Vicia faba (fava bean) protein hydrolysate; the speaker says it works three ways: building muscle (mTOR), protecting it from breakdown (ubiquitination) and calming inflammation (NF-κB) [03:56] (slide 8).

Immobilisation trial (Weijzen et al. 2023, The Journal of Nutrition; men aged 18-35, 20 g a day): muscle size changed the same as with milk protein concentrate, which was the control, not a placebo. Leg press strength recovered to 103% of baseline against 68% with milk protein, and muscle protein synthesis in recovery was about four times higher (read from the chart) [03:56] (slide 10).

Strength recovery trial (Kerr et al. 2023, Nutrients; men aged 30-45, 2.4 g a day for 17 days, muscle damage on day 14): peak torque was higher than placebo at 72 hours (p=0.025), with 36% less fatigue at 48 hours and 47% less at 72 hours (read from the chart) [03:56] (slide 11).

Strength and endurance trial (Mohan et al., BMJ Nutrition, Prevention & Health; men and women aged 19-40, 2.4 g a day for 56 days): leg extension 1RM higher at day 28 and day 56, endurance higher at day 56, bone mineral content up ("a serendipitous finding"), and 51.85% against 14.29% on placebo rated their health above 95 [03:56] (slide 12).

Nuritas positions PeptiStrong as a booster of protein and a partner for leucine, HMB and creatine: "we're not competing with protein". The leucine and HMB data are from muscle cells; the creatine case is in vitro data for each ingredient on its own [03:56] (slides 13, 14).

EU claims are protein claims ("source of protein" needs at least 12% of energy from protein), with US structure and function claims and brand callouts beside them; Vivatis Pharma and Tantus show a prototype PeptiStrong tablet with Nuritas [13:50] (slides 15, 17).

Ubiquinol is the reduced, active form of CoQ10. The speaker said the converting enzyme diaphorase is no longer available from about 30 [00:00]; the slide shows NQO1 activity falling 88% between 15 and 60 years (slide 2).

Blood levels after 28 days, read from the chart: 90 mg of ubiquinol about 2.8 µg/ml against about 2.7 for 300 mg of oxidised CoQ10; 300 mg of ubiquinol about 7.3 against about 3.2 for 900 mg of CoQ10 (slide 9). Spoken as equivalent at 90 against 300 mg [00:00].

Dose: 100 mg a day (to 200 mg for one month) to maintain energy levels; 300 mg to restore or boost energy and for fertility support (slide 11). Spoken, 300 mg is also for statin users and people under stress [00:00]; the slide names neither.

Sport: "Ubiquinol loading", every day for seven days before events such as marathons and triathlons and five days after, sits under the 300 mg dose (slide 11). The Energy and Sports block counts 16 studies, on energy and fatigue, oxidative stress, inflammation and muscle recovery (slide 13).

Formats: pure ubiquinol for softgels, liquid-filled hard capsules, gummies and beadlets; "ultra stabilized" ubiquinol for tablets, capsules, bars, shots, sticks, gels, gums and coffee or tea capsules (slide 12). Spoken as "a microencapsule form" [00:00].

Claimed evidence base: 100+ studies, 80+ patents, 45+ years of research; heart health 23 studies, healthy ageing and cognition 23, fertility 18, energy and sports 16, women and beauty from within 4 (slide 13).

NovaSOL is a micelle encapsulation technology: the active ingredient is the core, a food-grade liquid emulsification system the shell; it is water-soluble and made by physical processing only, with no chemical modification (slide 3) (slide 4) [00:18].
Each NovaSOL formula is unique to its ingredient; it is a water-free liquid concentrate for capsules and shots, and different NovaSOL formulations can be combined in capsules (slide 3) (slide 5).

Nugevia, a US direct-to-consumer brand, launched three combination products on Jotrol micellar resveratrol: MND with NovaSOL Curcumin, PWR with NovaSOL Q and GLO with NovaSOL Astaxanthin, in vegetarian SeaGel softgels, positioned in longevity (slide 7).
MSM is 34% sulfur by weight, a source of sulfur and methyl groups; supplementation "has shown" effects on joint and skin health and exercise recovery, the speaker said [10:40].
Balchem has 33 active research projects; methylfolate is a new ingredient it hopes to bring to Europe soon [09:04].
The gap he names is anabolic resistance: ageing muscle "responds less to protein and training", so protein advice rises from 0.8 to 1.2 g, and "hardly any ingredient" addresses it (slide 3) [00:00].

Wild Rhodiola rosea is overharvested and adulterated with non-rosea species. Rhodiola spp. has been in CITES Appendix II since February 2023, so roots and extracts traded across borders need CITES documents (slide 4). He said it was listed "as an endangered species"; the slide says CITES Appendix II, which differs [00:00].

In primary human muscle cells only the cultivated extract raised Pax7 and MyoD, the muscle stem-cell markers; wild harvest had no effect. Published as Iannuzzo et al., Antioxidants 2024;13:1000 (slide 8) [00:00].

Trial: 12 weeks, 140 inactive adults aged 55 to 75, RhoSera 400 mg a day or placebo, both arms on the same training programme plus 60 g protein a day (slide 9). He described it as double-blind and placebo-controlled [00:00].

Muscle soreness (DOMS) fell 46.3% in men and 51.7% in women, against 18.1% and 10.6% on placebo (slide 9, read from the chart); p = 0.004 and p < 0.001. He rounded these to 46%, 52%, 18% and 11% [00:00]. The data are "on file" and the manuscript is "in preparation" (slide 9).

No authorised EFSA claim for rhodiola. On-hold areas (stress, physical and mental performance) are usable if substantiated, per national rules; pair with magnesium or B vitamins for authorised fatigue claims (slide 11) [00:00].
The standard brief is "impossible"; judge a launch on whether they will remember it, whether you can make it and whether you can prove it [00:01] (slide 2) (slide 4).

items.text: Fermotein is 50% protein with a complete amino acid profile, 30% fibre ("unique fungal fibres"), spermidine at "7x more than wheat germ", vitamin B6, vitamin B4, calcium, iron, zinc, phosphorus and magnesium (slide 5). Spoken: chitin and chitosan fibre, spermidine at about 1,700 mg per kilo, seven times "beet germ" as transcribed, and choline [00:00].

Approvals: self-affirmed GRAS in the US and Singapore (SFA) approval in 2024, EFSA safety approval in 2025, EU authorisation and market launch in 2026 (slide 3). He said "since the summer of this year" after five years, with Australia and Canada pending [00:00].

All-in-one nutrition is worth $0.5 to 1bn in the US against $8.6bn for protein supplements and $4.9bn for meal replacement (2025), and is priced at about $5 to $7 a serving against $1 to $2 for protein powder and $4 to $6 for meal replacement (slide 6) [00:00].

Ka'Chava: $47.2M measured retail sales excluding direct sales, up 24.4% in dollars and 39.9% in units over 52 weeks to 07/12/2026 (SPINS); single-serve multipacks grow fastest, up 254% to over 1,000%, at the highest price per serving (slide 8). He called it "super profitable" [00:00].

Evidence is preclinical: in a TNO gut model Fermotein raised butyrate, propionate and acetate and microbial diversity; in TNO human colon tissue it raised GLP-1 against a blank; in NemaLife's C. elegans study median lifespan rose 21.7%, 28 against 23 days (slide 11) (slide 12). He said 22% [00:00].

Next: a 16-week human RCT on biological ageing clocks in adults aged 40 to 60, led by Dr Pol Grootswagers of Wageningen; a human spermidine bioavailability trial; and a NemaLife follow-up on lifespan and muscle health (slide 13). He said the ageing-clock trial starts in quarter one [00:00].

Mechanisms make promises and sell, but outcomes retain customers (slide 6). Shoppers ask whether and when they will feel it, whether they can measure it, and what it costs (slide 8); when trials show a benefit at four, six or eight weeks, H&B can sometimes put that on pack [00:25].

items.text: The market is framed as three sides, brands, manufacturers and ingredient suppliers, with Grand View Research's forecast of over 12 percent growth a year to more than 60 billion dollars by 2030 [00:13].
The cost of today's process is operational (hours organising inquiries, hunting agreements in email threads) and lost opportunity (offers never received, inquiries never answered) [01:50].
One inquiry reaches all manufacturers (or suppliers) in the category; offers come back in one structure, "two offers or 15", ready to compare [02:46].
For suppliers and manufacturers: inquiries are matched to what you can produce, so you see opportunities that today never find you [02:46].
Every company is verified before joining; the security module answers losing control of information once it sits in an inbox [07:42].
Pawel Gruszczynski (Remedy, the conference organiser) is strategic advisor and board member of the project [02:46].

Matt: trials in this industry study healthy people for short periods, so effects look small; he would run high-dose studies in people with real problems and publish, because consumers will find it through chatbots [02:52].
Alex: consumers want evidence but not the EFSA wording; "throwing the kitchen sink" (90 plus ingredients, 35 claims) muddles the message; do a few things well for a defined audience [08:33].

Joanna: EU food law and the claims regulation were written for vitamin C and D; innovators must combine what is legally possible with showing what trials found; food law should be "a shield", not "a heartbreak" [05:36].
Matt: same safety package, three years longer approval in Europe than the US; cost today, income later, so the delay "almost makes the innovation impossible" [14:53].
Matt: fish oil supply is collapsing for aquaculture now and reaches supplement shelves next summer; aquaculture buys the alternatives with higher willingness to pay [18:48].
Alex: H&B holds up to nine months of pre-purchased stock on core lines; shoppers give three or four seconds at shelf, so protect the claim they buy (heart, eye) and find the alternative [19:36].

Biotics have never been more popular: probiotic use among US adults rose 287% from 2009 to 2023, and European online probiotic sales have grown 15-25% a year since 2020 (slide 2). Yet in 7 of 8 European countries consumers do not feel informed about probiotics (slide 6); she said this without figures [00:24].

Her example sets expectations at week 1 and months 1, 2 and 3 (slide 17); she said "for one week, for one month" [03:59].

items.text: Rule 4, from supplement to everyday food and formats: products designed for the person, not the bacteria; "the best biotic is the one people actually take every day" (slide 18). Poppi is her example [03:59].
ingredients: Akkermansia (Pendulum, the US brand built on it; heard as "Acromancia")

items.text: In Europe you cannot claim most of it, so the brand carries it: BioGaia's baby drops say "for colic & digestive discomfort" in the US but "one of the world's most researched lactic acid bacteria strains" in Europe (slide 20), and Activia names its strain, Bifidus ActiRegularis (slide 21) [03:59].
ingredients: Akkermansia (Pendulum, the US brand built on it; heard as "Acromancia")

items.text: Novonesis pitches to CMOs and CDMOs directly: probiotic solutions "already supported by research, market experience, and technical know-how", with the aim of a product the consumer will trust and repurchase, not only an ingredient sale [00:42].
Science is strain specific; some strains have limited documentation, others decades of study, and documented strains protect the reputation of the brand the manufacturer makes [00:42].

Four probiotic trends: more specialised needs, professional-recommended probiotics, applications beyond gut health, digital channels and emerging markets; "probiotic are no longer a niche category" [00:42].

Lactoflorene: partnership since the early 2000s, started by an Italian requirement of at least 1 billion CFU in a limited-volume cap; Novonesis gave the potency and stability; core formula unchanged for almost 20 years; a clinical study on the finished product beyond what Italy demanded [09:06].

Lactoflorene is third in Italy with around a 7% share; the three reasons given were clinical evidence, delivery innovation (the MCAP system for liquid shots) and formats for different ages and occasions [09:06].
The partnership's value beyond ingredients: formulation expertise, consumer and marketing support, access to a pipeline of new bio-solutions [13:10].

Its pitch as a CDMO is speed and flexibility: a low time to market, agile family decisions, custom fermentation from 1 L to 40,000 L, and a new kind of production if asked (slide 6) (slide 8) [00:00].
ingredients: CA15 (Sacco, L. rhamnosus CA15 DSM 33960, patented strain)
Synbio (Sacco, patented mix of L. rhamnosus IMC 501 and L. paracasei IMC 502)

items.text: CA15 trials: two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies, 60 women in 2023 and 200 in 2025, one capsule of 10 billion CFU a day for 10 days and a 30-day wash-out (slide 14). They differ from the talk, which gave a six-woman exploratory study and "10 mil per capsule" [00:00].
ingredients: CA15 (Sacco, L. rhamnosus CA15 DSM 33960, patented strain)
Synbio (Sacco, patented mix of L. rhamnosus IMC 501 and L. paracasei IMC 502)

items.text: CA15 results: symptom scores fell 78% for discomfort, 66% burning, 64% itching, 62% secretions and 56% inflammation (slide 15). On the Amsel criteria 98% of women had a corrected pH, 92% a negative amine test, 79% no clue cells and 75% normal discharge, as labelled on the chart (slide 16); he gave the first three the same [00:00].
ingredients: CA15 (Sacco, L. rhamnosus CA15 DSM 33960, patented strain)
Synbio (Sacco, patented mix of L. rhamnosus IMC 501 and L. paracasei IMC 502)

items.text: Synbio trial: L. rhamnosus IMC 501 and L. paracasei IMC 502, 5 billion CFU a serving for six months in 97 healthy people over 65, randomised, double-blind and placebo-controlled (slide 21) (slide 23); spoken as "five mil" daily [00:00].

items.text: Synbio results, end of study against start: hs-CRP down 43%, IL-8 down 83%, IL-6 67%, MIP-1α 60% and TNF-α 23% (slide 25); total short-chain fatty acids up 23% and butyric acid up 33% (slide 26) [00:00].

items.text: Chewable probiotic: Compressol ProTab is a low water activity direct-compression platform that compresses at low force, so live cultures survive; the concept is an adult mint chew, "Gut Performance Chew" (slide 5) (slide 7) [00:01].
ingredients: Compressol ProTab (SPI Pharma; polyol-based chewable platform)

items.text: Effer-Soda is a surface-modified sodium bicarbonate, stable across packing forms, "not only desiccant tubes": 15–25% of a tablet or sachet formula as the effervescent system, or 1–4% for sparkle in a chewable or fast-melt; the concept is a fizzy electrolyte and energy stick for sport (slide 8) (slide 10) [00:01].

items.text: Fast-melt: Advantol 300 with Effer-Soda 12 disintegrates in under 10 seconds, 20–40% faster than typical direct-compression competitors, and uses standard packaging, not lyophilised blisters (slide 14) (slide 15). It is aimed at children and older people who cannot or will not swallow [00:01].
